blocks.content: Soil is the foundation of agriculture, vegetation, and human survival. In India, soil diversity is very high due to variations in relief, climate, parent rocks, vegetation, and time. Questions from soils of India are frequently asked in SSC in the form of direct questions, matching, assertion– reason, and applied concepts. This chapter explains soils from formation to classification, characteristics, distribution, crops, and problems in maximum possible detail.
PART A: BASIC CONCEPT OF SOIL

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Soil formation (pedogenesis) is a slow process involving physical, chemical, and biological weathering driven by parent material, climate, relief, vegetation, and time.
Alluvial soil is the most widespread and fertile soil in India, categorized into new alluvium (Khadar) and old alluvium (Bhangar).
Black soil (Regur) is derived from volcanic rocks, possesses high moisture retention, and exhibits a unique self-ploughing nature ideal for cotton.
Red soil owes its colour to iron oxide, while Laterite soil is formed in high temperature and heavy rainfall areas through intense leaching.
Soil erosion occurs via sheet, rill, gully, and wind mechanisms, but can be mitigated using conservation methods like contour ploughing, terracing, and afforestation.

blocks.content: Meaning of Soil

Soil is the uppermost layer of the Earth’s crust formed by the weathering of rocks and the decomposition of organic matter. It is a natural resource that supports plant growth and agricultural activities.
Soil Formation (Pedogenesis)
Soil formation is a slow process called pedogenesis. It involves physical, chemical, and biological weathering of rocks followed by the addition of organic matter.
Factors of Soil Formation
Soil formation depends on five major factors: Parent material, Climate, Relief, Vegetation, and Time. These factors together determine soil type and fertility.
PART B: CLASSIFICATION OF SOILS IN INDIA
Basis of Soil Classification in India
Indian soils are classified on the basis of origin, composition, colour, texture, and fertility.
Alluvial Soil
Alluvial soil is formed by the deposition of sediments brought by rivers. It is the most widespread and fertile soil in India.

Distribution: Northern plains of India, river valleys, deltas. Characteristics: Rich in potash and lime, poor in nitrogen. Types: Khadar (new alluvium) and Bhangar (old alluvium). Crops: Rice, wheat, sugarcane, maize, pulses.
Black Soil (Regur Soil)
Black soil is derived from volcanic rocks and is also known as regur soil. It has high moisture retention capacity.
Distribution: Deccan Plateau.
Characteristics: Rich in lime, iron, magnesium; poor in phosphorus. Special Feature: Self-ploughing nature.
Soil is the uppermost layer of the Earth’s crust formed by the weathering of rocks and the decomposition of organic matter.
Crops: Cotton, sugarcane, oilseeds.
Red Soil
Red soil develops on crystalline and metamorphic rocks. Its red colour is due to the presence of iron oxide.
Distribution: Southern and eastern India. Characteristics: Poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus. Crops: Millets, pulses, groundnut.
Laterite Soil
Laterite soil forms in regions with high temperature and heavy rainfall. It results from intense leaching.
Distribution: Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats, northeastern India. Characteristics: Acidic, poor fertility.
Crops: Tea, coffee, cashew.
Arid / Desert Soil

rows: Rich in potash and lime; divided into Khadar and Bhangar
High moisture retention, rich in iron/lime, self-ploughing
Red colour due to iron oxide; poor in nitrogen and humus
Intense leaching under high temp & rainfall
Acidic, low fertility due to leaching

blocks.content: Desert soil is found in arid regions with low rainfall. It contains high salt content.
Distribution: Rajasthan, Gujarat. Characteristics: Sandy, low moisture. Crops: Bajra, barley with irrigation.
Forest & Mountain Soil
Forest and mountain soils are found in hilly and mountainous regions. Their characteristics vary with altitude.
Distribution: Himalayas. Characteristics: Rich in humus, acidic. Crops: Tea, coffee, fruits.
Peaty & Marshy Soil
Peaty soils are found in areas of heavy rainfall and high humidity. They contain large amount of organic matter.
Distribution: Kerala, Sundarbans. Characteristics: Acidic, waterlogged. Crops: Rice.
Saline & Alkaline Soil
Saline soils contain high salt content and are infertile. They are formed due to excessive irrigation and evaporation.
PART C: SOIL EROSION & CONSERVATION
Soil Erosion
Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil by agents like water and wind. It reduces soil fertility.

items: Black soil is also known as Regur soil and is renowned for its self-ploughing nature and suitability for cotton.
The distinct red colour of Red soil is caused by the presence of iron oxide.
Khadar represents new alluvium deposition whereas Bhangar represents old alluvium deposition.
Laterite soil is formed due to intense leaching in regions experiencing high temperatures and heavy rainfall.

blocks.content: Types of Soil Erosion
Sheet erosion, rill erosion, gully erosion, wind erosion.
Soil Conservation Methods
Contour ploughing, terracing, afforestation, shelter belts, strip cropping.
PART D: IMPORTANCE OF SOIL
Soil is essential for agriculture, vegetation, food security, and ecological balance.
